front: What are urbanisation and urban growth?
p1: Urbanisation is the increasing proportion of people living in towns and cities.
p2: Urban growth is a rise in a town's population.
s: Urbanisation is the increasing proportion of people living in towns and cities.
Urban growth is a rise in a town's population.

front: How do rural-urban migration and natural increase make LIC and NEE cities grow?
p1: Rural-urban migration, the movement of people from the countryside to towns and cities, is the main reason LIC and NEE cities grow so fast.
p2: Natural increase happens when the birth rate is higher than the death rate.
s: Rural-urban migration, the movement of people from the countryside to towns and cities, is the main reason LIC and NEE cities grow so fast.
Natural increase happens when the birth rate is higher than the death rate.

front: What are slums and ragpickers?
p1: A slum has poor quality, often illegal housing that lacks clean water, sewers or electricity.
p2: Ragpickers recycle about 80% of Mumbai's waste, and collecting and recycling plastic in Dharavi creates hundreds of thousands of jobs.
s: A slum has poor quality, often illegal housing that lacks clean water, sewers or electricity.
Ragpickers recycle about 80% of Mumbai's waste, and collecting and recycling plastic in Dharavi creates hundreds of thousands of jobs.

front: What is the informal sector?
p1: Informal jobs, such as hawkers and laundry workers, have no contracts, no legal protections and little job security.
p2: The informal sector is not taxed by the government, so the city cannot gain taxes.
s: Informal jobs, such as hawkers and laundry workers, have no contracts, no legal protections and little job security.
The informal sector is not taxed by the government, so the city cannot gain taxes.

front: Where is Mumbai?
p1: Mumbai is in Asia → India → the state of Maharashtra; it is the state capital, but NOT the capital of India.
p2: Mumbai lies on the west coast of India, not the east; its port handles 70% of maritime trade and 3 million people commute in from surrounding areas.
p3: Mumbai has a population of over 21 million → India's largest city and a megacity (10 million+ people).
s: Mumbai is in Asia → India → the state of Maharashtra; it is the state capital, but NOT the capital of India.
Mumbai lies on the west coast of India, not the east; its port handles 70% of maritime trade and 3 million people commute in from surrounding areas.
Mumbai has a population of over 21 million → India's largest city and a megacity (10 million+ people).

front: Why is Mumbai important?
p1: Regional: capital of Maharashtra → generates 40% of the state's income; 3 million people commute in from surrounding areas.
p2: National: commercial capital of India → 6% of India's GDP; home to the Bombay Stock Exchange, Reserve Bank of India and Tata Group; its port handles 70% of maritime trade.
p3: International: a top ten world centre of commerce; Bollywood is the largest film producer in the world; its history with Portugal and Britain makes it a melting pot of cultures.
s: Regional: capital of Maharashtra → generates 40% of the state's income; 3 million people commute in from surrounding areas.
National: commercial capital of India → 6% of India's GDP; home to the Bombay Stock Exchange, Reserve Bank of India and Tata Group; its port handles 70% of maritime trade.
International: a top ten world centre of commerce; Bollywood is the largest film producer in the world; its history with Portugal and Britain makes it a melting pot of cultures.

front: Why is Mumbai growing so rapidly?
p1: Rural-urban migration is the first cause → 480 migrants arrive in Mumbai each day.
p2: Push: average wage in rural Maharashtra is as low as $1 a day; pull: it is $20 a day in Mumbai, though less in the informal sector.
p3: Natural increase is the second cause → a high birth rate; it is birth rate minus death rate.
s: Rural-urban migration is the first cause → 480 migrants arrive in Mumbai each day.
Push: average wage in rural Maharashtra is as low as $1 a day; pull: it is $20 a day in Mumbai, though less in the informal sector.
Natural increase is the second cause → a high birth rate; it is birth rate minus death rate.

front: What opportunities does Mumbai offer?
p1: Education: primary and secondary schools with free education up to certain ages; University of Mumbai is world renowned; literacy rate 89.7% (slums: 69%+).
p2: Health and resources: healthcare is better than the rest of India; 98% of people have electricity and water supply.
p3: Industry: Bombay Stock Exchange and Tata Group; informal jobs in recycling, leather tanning and pottery; call centres in Navi Mumbai after government tax breaks and IT parks.
s: Education: primary and secondary schools with free education up to certain ages; University of Mumbai is world renowned; literacy rate 89.7% (slums: 69%+).
Health and resources: healthcare is better than the rest of India; 98% of people have electricity and water supply.
Industry: Bombay Stock Exchange and Tata Group; informal jobs in recycling, leather tanning and pottery; call centres in Navi Mumbai after government tax breaks and IT parks.

front: What challenges does Dharavi face?
p1: Dharavi is one of the largest slums in Asia, in the heart of Mumbai → overcrowding with about a million people.
p2: 500 people share one public toilet and open sewers run through the streets → water-borne disease such as typhoid and diphtheria.
p3: One third of residents have experienced crime; residents have no legal right to the land → it can be cleared at any time.
s: Dharavi is one of the largest slums in Asia, in the heart of Mumbai → overcrowding with about a million people.
500 people share one public toilet and open sewers run through the streets → water-borne disease such as typhoid and diphtheria.
One third of residents have experienced crime; residents have no legal right to the land → it can be cleared at any time.

front: Why do sanitation and waste cause problems in Dharavi?
p1: Slum areas often lack proper sewage, so dirty water flows into the river; water-borne disease spreads, including cholera where rubbish dumps infect water supplies.
p2: There is no proper city-wide rubbish collection, and none organised in Dharavi, so open dumps attract rats and cockroaches → disease.
p3: Positive: ragpickers collect and recycle plastic → this creates hundreds of thousands of jobs.
s: Slum areas often lack proper sewage, so dirty water flows into the river; water-borne disease spreads, including cholera where rubbish dumps infect water supplies.
There is no proper city-wide rubbish collection, and none organised in Dharavi, so open dumps attract rats and cockroaches → disease.
Positive: ragpickers collect and recycle plastic → this creates hundreds of thousands of jobs.

front: How is informal work both a strength and a problem?
p1: Strength: thousands of small workshops and home businesses in Dharavi do recycling, leather tanning and pottery work for residents.
p2: Problem: informal work has no contracts, no legal protections and little job security; it is not taxed by the government → the city cannot gain taxes.
p3: Problem: it traps many residents in low-income, unstable work → young people leave education early to work.
s: Strength: thousands of small workshops and home businesses in Dharavi do recycling, leather tanning and pottery work for residents.
Problem: informal work has no contracts, no legal protections and little job security; it is not taxed by the government → the city cannot gain taxes.
Problem: it traps many residents in low-income, unstable work → young people leave education early to work.

front: How polluted are Mumbai's water and air?
p1: The Mithi River flows through the city including Dharavi; 93% of its waste comes from homes and 7% from factories.
p2: About 1,500 factories line the river and many release waste straight in → Water Quality Index 'bad to very bad'.
p3: Smog is common and particulate matter is 15x over the safe limit → asthma and other serious health problems; Mumbai is ranked 4th most polluted megacity in the world.
s: The Mithi River flows through the city including Dharavi; 93% of its waste comes from homes and 7% from factories.
About 1,500 factories line the river and many release waste straight in → Water Quality Index 'bad to very bad'.
Smog is common and particulate matter is 15x over the safe limit → asthma and other serious health problems; Mumbai is ranked 4th most polluted megacity in the world.

front: How bad is traffic congestion in Mumbai?
p1: Mumbai has 1.8 million motor vehicles; private vehicles are up by more than half in 8 years and people spend about 1.5 hours a day stuck in traffic.
p2: Trains built for 1,700 passengers often carry three times that number, so overcrowding is severe on the rail network.
p3: Response: nearly 90% use public transport; a new traffic system is run from a control centre in Mumbai police headquarters.
s: Mumbai has 1.8 million motor vehicles; private vehicles are up by more than half in 8 years and people spend about 1.5 hours a day stuck in traffic.
Trains built for 1,700 passengers often carry three times that number, so overcrowding is severe on the rail network.
Response: nearly 90% use public transport; a new traffic system is run from a control centre in Mumbai police headquarters.

front: How does the Dharavi Sector 5 redevelopment change quality of life?
p1: A $2 billion project in Sector 5 of Dharavi → slum housing demolished and replaced by high-rise tower blocks; 72,000 families rehomed.
p2: Improved: proper plumbing and toilets → less water-borne disease, e.g. cholera; new parks and green space; secure windows and doors.
p3: Worsened: most slum dwellers have no legal right to land → homeless; loss of community (some families there 150 years); flats too small (5 to 10 people in 21 m2).
s: A $2 billion project in Sector 5 of Dharavi → slum housing demolished and replaced by high-rise tower blocks; 72,000 families rehomed.
Improved: proper plumbing and toilets → less water-borne disease, e.g. cholera; new parks and green space; secure windows and doors.
Worsened: most slum dwellers have no legal right to land → homeless; loss of community (some families there 150 years); flats too small (5 to 10 people in 21 m2).

front: What are the parts of an ecosystem?
p1: An ecosystem is made up of producers, consumers and decomposers interacting with each other and with the non-living parts of the environment.
p2: A producer is a plant that uses sunlight, water and carbon dioxide to make its own food.
p3: A decomposer breaks down dead organisms and returns nutrients to the soil.
s: An ecosystem is made up of producers, consumers and decomposers interacting with each other and with the non-living parts of the environment.
A producer is a plant that uses sunlight, water and carbon dioxide to make its own food.
A decomposer breaks down dead organisms and returns nutrients to the soil.

front: What are primary and secondary consumers?
p1: A primary consumer feeds on producers, so it is a herbivore.
p2: A secondary consumer feeds on primary consumers, so it is a carnivore.
s: A primary consumer feeds on producers, so it is a herbivore.
A secondary consumer feeds on primary consumers, so it is a carnivore.

front: What are food chains and food webs?
p1: A food chain shows how each living thing gets its food, starting with plants.
p2: A food web is made of interlocking food chains.
s: A food chain shows how each living thing gets its food, starting with plants.
A food web is made of interlocking food chains.

front: What are biodiversity and biomes?
p1: Biodiversity is the variety of life in an area.
p2: A biome is a large area with similar climate, geology and vegetation, found in bands of latitude around the planet.
s: Biodiversity is the variety of life in an area.
A biome is a large area with similar climate, geology and vegetation, found in bands of latitude around the planet.

front: What are differential heating and the Hadley cell?
p1: Differential heating is the term that explains why it is hotter at the Equator than at the Poles.
p2: The Hadley cell is the loop of rising and sinking air between the equator and about 30 degrees north and south.
p3: Air rises at the equator, cools, condenses and falls as heavy rain, then sinks at 30 degrees, bringing high pressure and almost no rain.
s: Differential heating is the term that explains why it is hotter at the Equator than at the Poles.
The Hadley cell is the loop of rising and sinking air between the equator and about 30 degrees north and south.
Air rises at the equator, cools, condenses and falls as heavy rain, then sinks at 30 degrees, bringing high pressure and almost no rain.

front: Why are rainforests on the equator and deserts near 30 degrees?
p1: The equator is heated intensely by differential heating, so it is hotter than the poles → temperature changes with latitude.
p2: At the equator air rises → cools → condenses → heavy convectional rain; this low pressure zone is the ITCZ (inter-tropical convergence zone).
p3: Air spreads north and south, cools and sinks at about 30 degrees N and S → high pressure → almost no rain → deserts; this loop is the Hadley cell.
s: The equator is heated intensely by differential heating, so it is hotter than the poles → temperature changes with latitude.
At the equator air rises → cools → condenses → heavy convectional rain; this low pressure zone is the ITCZ (inter-tropical convergence zone).
Air spreads north and south, cools and sinks at about 30 degrees N and S → high pressure → almost no rain → deserts; this loop is the Hadley cell.

front: How will climate change affect Epping Forest?
p1: Epping Forest is deciduous woodland, the most common ecosystem in the UK → the trees lose their leaves each year.
p2: Wetter summers and milder temperatures → oak mildew weakens oaks (Oak Decline); warmer winters let insects survive all year → pests rise, e.g. Horse Chestnut Leaf Miner.
p3: Windthrow: more wind and wet soils → trees uprooted; the cause is the burning of fossil fuels, which releases carbon dioxide.
s: Epping Forest is deciduous woodland, the most common ecosystem in the UK → the trees lose their leaves each year.
Wetter summers and milder temperatures → oak mildew weakens oaks (Oak Decline); warmer winters let insects survive all year → pests rise, e.g. Horse Chestnut Leaf Miner.
Windthrow: more wind and wet soils → trees uprooted; the cause is the burning of fossil fuels, which releases carbon dioxide.

front: What is a tropical rainforest like?
p1: Found on or around the equator; the Amazon is the world's largest tropical rainforest, spanning 9 countries in South America with 60% in Brazil.
p2: Climate: hot and wet all year with a very small temperature range; rain falls in every month.
p3: Structure: four layers, with emergent trees 40 to 60 m tall; biodiversity is very high, with 6% of the Earth but around 50% of known species.
s: Found on or around the equator; the Amazon is the world's largest tropical rainforest, spanning 9 countries in South America with 60% in Brazil.
Climate: hot and wet all year with a very small temperature range; rain falls in every month.
Structure: four layers, with emergent trees 40 to 60 m tall; biodiversity is very high, with 6% of the Earth but around 50% of known species.

front: Why is the rainforest climate hot and wet?
p1: The sun is overhead at the equator → energy is concentrated on a small surface area; the wettest month is March, with about 314 mm.
p2: Evaporation is rapid, so warm moist air rises → low pressure.
p3: Rising air cools → condensation → clouds → heavy convectional rain, usually in the afternoon; the equator has rising air in the Hadley cell, the ITCZ.
s: The sun is overhead at the equator → energy is concentrated on a small surface area; the wettest month is March, with about 314 mm.
Evaporation is rapid, so warm moist air rises → low pressure.
Rising air cools → condensation → clouds → heavy convectional rain, usually in the afternoon; the equator has rising air in the Hadley cell, the ITCZ.

front: How are rainforest plants adapted?
p1: Emergent trees are very tall (40 to 60 m) → reach the strongest sunlight above the canopy; buttress roots act as an anchor → support tall emergent trees.
p2: Drip tips are pointed leaf ends → heavy rain runs off quickly so leaves are not damaged; glossy, pointed-tip leaves in the canopy repel water.
p3: Canopy plants encase seeds in fruit → animals eat it and spread seeds; emergent trees have lightweight seeds spread by wind; understorey plants have larger leaves for dim light.
s: Emergent trees are very tall (40 to 60 m) → reach the strongest sunlight above the canopy; buttress roots act as an anchor → support tall emergent trees.
Drip tips are pointed leaf ends → heavy rain runs off quickly so leaves are not damaged; glossy, pointed-tip leaves in the canopy repel water.
Canopy plants encase seeds in fruit → animals eat it and spread seeds; emergent trees have lightweight seeds spread by wind; understorey plants have larger leaves for dim light.

front: How are rainforest animals adapted?
p1: Emergent layer animals fly or glide, e.g. birds, bats, gliders and butterflies.
p2: Most animals live in the canopy because there is plenty of fruit; the Boto (pink river dolphin) lives in Amazon freshwater habitats.
p3: Decomposers such as termites, slugs, worms and fungi live on the forest floor.
s: Emergent layer animals fly or glide, e.g. birds, bats, gliders and butterflies.
Most animals live in the canopy because there is plenty of fruit; the Boto (pink river dolphin) lives in Amazon freshwater habitats.
Decomposers such as termites, slugs, worms and fungi live on the forest floor.

front: Why is rainforest soil nutrient-rich but fragile?
p1: The soil is nutrient-rich but shallow, and the trees shed their leaves all year.
p2: Dead leaves break down rapidly on the warm damp floor with insects, forming humus that roots absorb quickly → nutrients are used up quickly.
p3: After clearance there is no canopy → heavy rain washes nutrients out and topsoil into rivers → the soil quickly becomes infertile and cleared land is often abandoned.
s: The soil is nutrient-rich but shallow, and the trees shed their leaves all year.
Dead leaves break down rapidly on the warm damp floor with insects, forming humus that roots absorb quickly → nutrients are used up quickly.
After clearance there is no canopy → heavy rain washes nutrients out and topsoil into rivers → the soil quickly becomes infertile and cleared land is often abandoned.

front: What causes deforestation in the Amazon?
p1: Causes: cattle ranching, commercial farming, subsistence farming, logging, mining, roads, settlement and energy (dams).
p2: Commercial: around 80% of cleared land becomes cattle pasture, with plantations of soya, palm oil and bananas; Brazil is one of the world's largest exporters.
p3: Subsistence: Amerindians have long used slash and burn → trees cut and burned for temporary nutrient-rich soil; government gave small amounts of land to some of Brazil's 25 million people.
s: Causes: cattle ranching, commercial farming, subsistence farming, logging, mining, roads, settlement and energy (dams).
Commercial: around 80% of cleared land becomes cattle pasture, with plantations of soya, palm oil and bananas; Brazil is one of the world's largest exporters.
Subsistence: Amerindians have long used slash and burn → trees cut and burned for temporary nutrient-rich soil; government gave small amounts of land to some of Brazil's 25 million people.

front: How do logging, mining, roads and dams clear the rainforest?
p1: Logging takes hardwoods such as mahogany for furniture; mining takes iron ore, bauxite and gold, with about 50,000 hectares cleared for gold alone (70,000 football pitches).
p2: Over 12,000 km of new roads have been built, including the Trans-Amazonian Highway (5,300 km) → opens remote areas.
p3: Brazil's population has more than doubled since 1972 and Parauapebas is fast-growing; 74 dams are on Amazon rivers, including Belo Monte (2019).
s: Logging takes hardwoods such as mahogany for furniture; mining takes iron ore, bauxite and gold, with about 50,000 hectares cleared for gold alone (70,000 football pitches).
Over 12,000 km of new roads have been built, including the Trans-Amazonian Highway (5,300 km) → opens remote areas.
Brazil's population has more than doubled since 1972 and Parauapebas is fast-growing; 74 dams are on Amazon rivers, including Belo Monte (2019).

front: What are the impacts of deforestation?
p1: Loss of biodiversity: 137 species lost a day; loss of indigenous people: about 6 million Amerindians in 1500, roughly 200,000 now.
p2: Without a canopy and roots, topsoil is washed away → soil erosion; nutrients are leached within a few years → infertile soil and abandoned land.
p3: Fewer trees → less evapotranspiration and rainfall, so parts of the forest risk turning to savanna; burning trees releases carbon (about 100 billion tonnes stored) → faster global warming.
s: Loss of biodiversity: 137 species lost a day; loss of indigenous people: about 6 million Amerindians in 1500, roughly 200,000 now.
Without a canopy and roots, topsoil is washed away → soil erosion; nutrients are leached within a few years → infertile soil and abandoned land.
Fewer trees → less evapotranspiration and rainfall, so parts of the forest risk turning to savanna; burning trees releases carbon (about 100 billion tonnes stored) → faster global warming.

front: Why are tropical rainforests valuable?
p1: Environment: the forest stores carbon and drives its own water cycle through evapotranspiration; it covers 6% of the Earth but holds around 50% of known species.
p2: Medicines: about 25% of modern medicines come from rainforest plants; the rosy periwinkle treats childhood leukaemia.
p3: People: timber, minerals, farmland, energy and jobs for Brazil; the forest is home to Amerindian groups such as the Kayapo (food, shelter, medicine).
s: Environment: the forest stores carbon and drives its own water cycle through evapotranspiration; it covers 6% of the Earth but holds around 50% of known species.
Medicines: about 25% of modern medicines come from rainforest plants; the rosy periwinkle treats childhood leukaemia.
People: timber, minerals, farmland, energy and jobs for Brazil; the forest is home to Amerindian groups such as the Kayapo (food, shelter, medicine).

front: How can the rainforest be managed sustainably?
p1: Sustainable management means meeting today's needs without damaging the resource for future generations.
p2: Local strategies are ecotourism, and selective logging with replanting; national parks work at national scale, e.g. Tumucumaque National Park (2002), around the size of Switzerland.
p3: International strategies are the timber agreement (ITTA) and debt reduction; charities such as WWF run conservation and education.
s: Sustainable management means meeting today's needs without damaging the resource for future generations.
Local strategies are ecotourism, and selective logging with replanting; national parks work at national scale, e.g. Tumucumaque National Park (2002), around the size of Switzerland.
International strategies are the timber agreement (ITTA) and debt reduction; charities such as WWF run conservation and education.

front: What are the pros and cons of local rainforest management?
p1: Ecotourism uses small, locally owned resorts of sustainable materials with local guides → money goes to local people, so the forest is worth more standing than cleared.
p2: Limit: ecotourism reaches only a few thousand people a year in the Amazon.
p3: Selective logging cuts only mature or valuable trees so the forest can recover; but felled trees damage others and secondary forest takes over 20 years to regain 80% of biodiversity.
s: Ecotourism uses small, locally owned resorts of sustainable materials with local guides → money goes to local people, so the forest is worth more standing than cleared.
Limit: ecotourism reaches only a few thousand people a year in the Amazon.
Selective logging cuts only mature or valuable trees so the forest can recover; but felled trees damage others and secondary forest takes over 20 years to regain 80% of biodiversity.

front: How do national parks and education help, and what are their limits?
p1: Tumucumaque National Park (2002) is around the size of Switzerland → it is hard to police illegal logging across such an area.
p2: WWF staff visit schools in rainforest areas to teach why the rainforest matters → this changes attitudes in the long term.
p3: Charities rely on donations, results take a long time, and many people cut forest because they are desperately poor.
s: Tumucumaque National Park (2002) is around the size of Switzerland → it is hard to police illegal logging across such an area.
WWF staff visit schools in rainforest areas to teach why the rainforest matters → this changes attitudes in the long term.

front: How do international agreements protect the rainforest?
p1: The International Tropical Timber Agreement (ITTA, 2006) marks hardwood with a registration number proving it came from a managed forest → illegal loggers find it harder to sell wood.
p2: Limits: some illegal timber still reaches market; remote areas are hard to monitor; people who rely on illegal logging lose income.
p3: In a debt-for-nature swap an HIC cancels an LIC or NEE's debt for protecting its forest; but the country loses income from it and the promise is hard to enforce.
s: The International Tropical Timber Agreement (ITTA, 2006) marks hardwood with a registration number proving it came from a managed forest → illegal loggers find it harder to sell wood.
Limits: some illegal timber still reaches market; remote areas are hard to monitor; people who rely on illegal logging lose income.
In a debt-for-nature swap an HIC cancels an LIC or NEE's debt for protecting its forest; but the country loses income from it and the promise is hard to enforce.

front: Where are rainforest, desert and savannah biomes?
p1: Tropical rainforest is very hot and wet, and found on or around the equator.
p2: Desert is very hot and very dry, and found around 30 degrees north and south.
p3: Tropical savannah is hot, dry grassland with scattered shrubs and trees, between rainforest and desert.
s: Tropical rainforest is very hot and wet, and found on or around the equator.
Desert is very hot and very dry, and found around 30 degrees north and south.
Tropical savannah is hot, dry grassland with scattered shrubs and trees, between rainforest and desert.

front: Where are tundra, taiga and deciduous biomes?
p1: Tundra is below freezing at night all year, known as land with no trees.
p2: Coniferous forest, or taiga, is northern evergreen forest.
p3: Temperate deciduous forest has four distinct seasons.
s: Tundra is below freezing at night all year, known as land with no trees.
Coniferous forest, or taiga, is northern evergreen forest.
Temperate deciduous forest has four distinct seasons.

front: What are resources and sustainable management?
p1: Resources are physical supplies that humans need to survive.
p2: Sustainable management means meeting the needs of today without damaging a resource for future generations.
s: Resources are physical supplies that humans need to survive.
Sustainable management means meeting the needs of today without damaging a resource for future generations.

front: What are energy security and the energy mix?
p1: Energy security means uninterrupted availability of energy sources at an affordable price.
p2: An energy mix is the combination of energy sources used to meet a country's total energy demand.
s: Energy security means uninterrupted availability of energy sources at an affordable price.
An energy mix is the combination of energy sources used to meet a country's total energy demand.

front: What is water stress and how do water transfer schemes help?
p1: Water stress is when a place's water demand cannot be met, so it is in deficit.
p2: A water transfer scheme moves water from surplus areas to deficit areas, such as Kielder Water reservoir in Northumberland.
s: Water stress is when a place's water demand cannot be met, so it is in deficit.
A water transfer scheme moves water from surplus areas to deficit areas, such as Kielder Water reservoir in Northumberland.

front: Why do energy security and resources matter?
p1: A regular supply of food, water and energy is essential for health, a good life, good social relations, security and freedom of choice → quality of life and economic well-being improve.
p2: An energy secure country has a reliable and uninterrupted supply, an affordable and competitively priced supply, and an accessible and available supply.
p3: It also has a domestic energy mix not reliant on imports; countries can generate their own energy or import it; the war in Ukraine linked energy security to the cost of living.
s: A regular supply of food, water and energy is essential for health, a good life, good social relations, security and freedom of choice → quality of life and economic well-being improve.

It also has a domestic energy mix not reliant on imports; countries can generate their own energy or import it; the war in Ukraine linked energy security to the cost of living.

front: What factors affect energy supply?
p1: Physical: just 1% of the Sahara would provide enough solar energy for the world; Iceland has hot rocks near the surface on a constructive boundary → geothermal energy.
p2: North Sea gas is mostly extracted → harder and costlier to get more; the USA is energy secure through fracking (shale gas).
p3: Pirates seized an oil tanker off Somalia; Germany plans to stop nuclear power (waste concerns); the Nembe Creek pipeline in the Niger delta had 53 leaks from suspected oil thieves.

front: How have UK food habits changed?
p1: Before the 1950s food was mostly seasonal; from the 1950s agribusiness grew and food costs fell, with environmental and social impacts.
p2: In 1951 the first UK supermarket opened in Streatham → supermarkets gained control of supply chains; globalisation brought strawberries in January from polytunnels in southern Spain.
p3: From the 1990s some people buy local food and demand for organic food has grown; lower food miles mean lower greenhouse gas emissions.
s: Before the 1950s food was mostly seasonal; from the 1950s agribusiness grew and food costs fell, with environmental and social impacts.
In 1951 the first UK supermarket opened in Streatham → supermarkets gained control of supply chains; globalisation brought strawberries in January from polytunnels in southern Spain.

front: Where does the UK's water come from?
p1: Surface water comes from rivers, lakes and reservoirs: 474 sources in England and Wales and 339 in Scotland.
p2: Surface water supplies 64% of England's drinking water and nearly 93% of Wales's.
p3: Groundwater is stored in aquifers (rock, sand and soil): 2,259 sources in England and Wales and 86 in Scotland, but only 30% of England's and 6% of Wales's tap water.
s: Surface water comes from rivers, lakes and reservoirs: 474 sources in England and Wales and 339 in Scotland.
Surface water supplies 64% of England's drinking water and nearly 93% of Wales's.

front: Why does a wet country worry about drought?
p1: Some areas of the UK have a water surplus while others have a deficit.
p2: London and 70% of English regions could be under water stress within two decades → severe unless action is taken.
p3: Water transfer schemes move water from surplus areas to deficit areas, e.g. Kielder Water reservoir in Northumberland, released into rivers → Newcastle, Sunderland, Durham, Darlington and Middlesbrough.
s: Some areas of the UK have a water surplus while others have a deficit.
London and 70% of English regions could be under water stress within two decades → severe unless action is taken.

Water transfer schemes move water from surplus areas to deficit areas, e.g. Kielder Water reservoir in Northumberland, released into rivers → Newcastle, Sunderland, Durham, Darlington and Middlesbrough.

front: Why have water transfer schemes been limited in the UK?
p1: A national water grid (like the electricity grid) has been considered but not developed.
p2: About 5% of UK supply is piped from outside the local area.
p3: Transfer schemes have fallen out of favour because of environmental impact on the donor area, cost and energy use.
s: A national water grid (like the electricity grid) has been considered but not developed.
About 5% of UK supply is piped from outside the local area.
Transfer schemes have fallen out of favour because of environmental impact on the donor area, cost and energy use.

front: Where are the Sahara and the Sahel?
p1: The Sahara covers 9,200,000 km², lies 15 to 30° north of the Equator and covers most of northern Africa.
p2: The Sahel is found on the fringe of a hot desert, the Sahara.
s: The Sahara covers 9,200,000 km², lies 15 to 30° north of the Equator and covers most of northern Africa.
The Sahel is found on the fringe of a hot desert, the Sahara.

front: What are the key terms for hot deserts?
p1: A desert is land or climate that is so dry it supports little vegetation.
p2: Arid land receives less than 250mm of precipitation a year, so it has very little vegetation.
p3: Erosion is when rock or soil is worn away and removed by wind, water or ice.
s: A desert is land or climate that is so dry it supports little vegetation.
Arid land receives less than 250mm of precipitation a year, so it has very little vegetation.
Erosion is when rock or soil is worn away and removed by wind, water or ice.

front: What is shown on a climate graph?
p1: Precipitation is any water that forms in the Earth's atmosphere and then drops onto the surface, such as rain, snow, sleet or hail.
p2: A climate graph shows temperature as a line graph and precipitation as a bar graph.
s: Precipitation is any water that forms in the Earth's atmosphere and then drops onto the surface, such as rain, snow, sleet or hail.
A climate graph shows temperature as a line graph and precipitation as a bar graph.

front: What are the diurnal range and a rainfall index?
p1: The diurnal range is the difference in temperature within one day.
p2: A rainfall index shows how much rainfall is above or below the long-term average.
s: The diurnal range is the difference in temperature within one day.
A rainfall index shows how much rainfall is above or below the long-term average.

front: What is the difference between weather and climate?
p1: Weather describes the day-to-day conditions of the atmosphere.
p2: Climate describes average weather conditions over longer periods of time.
s: Weather describes the day-to-day conditions of the atmosphere.
Climate describes average weather conditions over longer periods of time.

front: What are xerophytes and ephemeral plants?
p1: Xerophytes are plants with physical adaptations to survive extreme heat and lack of water, such as the saguaro cactus.
p2: Ephemeral plants have behavioural adaptations, such as the ocotillo, which becomes dormant during dry periods and springs to life when water becomes available.
s: Xerophytes are plants with physical adaptations to survive extreme heat and lack of water, such as the saguaro cactus.
Ephemeral plants have behavioural adaptations, such as the ocotillo, which becomes dormant during dry periods and springs to life when water becomes available.

front: What does nocturnal mean?
p1: A nocturnal animal comes out at night.
p2: The leopard gecko is strictly nocturnal, sleeping during the day to limit its exposure to the heat of the sun.
s: A nocturnal animal comes out at night.
The leopard gecko is strictly nocturnal, sleeping during the day to limit its exposure to the heat of the sun.

front: What is appropriate technology?
p1: Appropriate technology is cheap to make, easy to use and easy to build or mend.
p2: It often takes advantage of local conditions, such as a sunny climate.
s: Appropriate technology is cheap to make, easy to use and easy to build or mend.
It often takes advantage of local conditions, such as a sunny climate.

front: How do plants adapt to hot deserts?
p1: Xerophytes have physical adaptations, e.g. the saguaro cactus → shallow roots (4 to 6 inches) catch rare rain, the fleshy stem stores water, thin spines replace leaves → less transpiration.
p2: The mesquite tree has tap roots as long as 24 metres → they reach the water table; small, waxy leaves cut water loss and leaves are dropped in droughts.
p3: Ephemerals have behavioural adaptations, e.g. the ocotillo → dormant in dry periods, new leaves after rain, waxy stem coating seals in moisture, up to five cycles a year.

front: How do animals adapt to hot deserts?
p1: Fennec fox → large ears dissipate excess body heat, kidneys restrict water loss, sandy colour reflects the Sun's heat, thick fur on the soles protects against hot sand.
p2: Leopard gecko → strictly nocturnal, sleeping by day to limit heat exposure; transparent eyelids protect against sandstorms; solid, crystallised faeces limit water loss.
p3: Gila monster → spends up to 98% of its life in burrows to avoid extreme heat; African elephant → huge ears with surface blood vessels cool its blood.

front: How is energy developed in the Sahara?
p1: Oil was found at Hassi Messaoud in 1956 → now one of North Africa's biggest oilfields, employing 40,000 local people, with Shell and BP.
p2: Challenges → deep in the Sahara, miles from roads, nearest oasis over 40 miles away; overcome by pumping water from aquifers and building a runway.
p3: Noor Ouarzazate in Morocco is a solar complex of about 580 MW → 8,500 construction jobs but only 234 permanent by 2022; mirrors cleaned with piped water.

front: How do mining and tourism help Morocco?
p1: Morocco is the world's leading exporter of phosphate, holding 75% of global reserves; mining gives about 10% of GDP; it is vital in synthetic fertiliser.
p2: Mining challenges → toxic risks to workers' health and the environment; mining is very water intensive → the company OCP builds desalination plants to supply fresh water.

front: Which other strategies reduce desertification?
p1: Solar cookers use free solar energy so women need not collect firewood → less deforestation; they are cheap and simple, but food cooks slowly and must be left outside.
p2: Crop rotation → farmers are taught about nutrients and soil exhaustion; legumes such as peas and beans are nitrogen fixers that boost soil fertility.
p3: Crop rotation is cheap but relies on a robust education system or NGOs; skills can be passed to other villages and to the farmers' children.

front: How does afforestation slow desertification?
p1: Planting trees stops and reverses desertification by preventing soil erosion, holding water in the soil and adding nutrients from decomposing leaf litter.
p2: The canopy increases humidity and offers shade, and native trees such as acacia are drought resilient.
p3: The African Union's Great Green Wall, launched in 2007, will cover 11 countries and measure 8,000 km long.

front: How do stone lines help in the Sahel?
p1: Stones are laid along the contours of the land in long lines, sometimes called bunds, 25 to 30 cm high.
p2: They slow run-off, so there is less soil erosion, and water pools behind the bund and soaks into the ground, trapping nutrients.
p3: The technique is low cost and spread from Burkina Faso to Mali and Niger, but reduced rainfall from climate change may stop it working properly.

front: What is standard of living?
p1: Standard of living is how much money and material wealth people have, and what that money can buy.
p2: It is about income, housing, food and access to goods and services, and is mostly measurable, such as GDP per capita, wages and electricity access.
s: Standard of living is how much money and material wealth people have, and what that money can buy.
It is about income, housing, food and access to goods and services, and is mostly measurable, such as GDP per capita, wages and electricity access.

front: What is quality of life?
p1: Quality of life is how good life feels and how satisfied people are with it.
p2: It includes things money cannot fully buy, such as health, safety, happiness, a clean environment, community, freedom and leisure time, so it is more subjective and harder to measure.
s: Quality of life is how good life feels and how satisfied people are with it.
It includes things money cannot fully buy, such as health, safety, happiness, a clean environment, community, freedom and leisure time, so it is more subjective and harder to measure.

front: What do LIC, NEE and HIC stand for?
p1: LIC stands for low income country.
p2: HIC stands for high income country.
p3: NEE stands for newly emerging economy; it is not a World Bank category but geographers use it for middle income countries that are developing quickly.
s: LIC stands for low income country.
HIC stands for high income country.
NEE stands for newly emerging economy; it is not a World Bank category but geographers use it for middle income countries that are developing quickly.

front: What is a development indicator?
p1: Development indicators are measurable statistics used to assess and compare the progress or quality of life of different regions or countries.
p2: Economic indicators measure the health of an economy, social indicators measure wider quality of life, and composite indicators combine several indicators for a more balanced judgement.
s: Development indicators are measurable statistics used to assess and compare the progress or quality of life of different regions or countries.
Economic indicators measure the health of an economy, social indicators measure wider quality of life, and composite indicators combine several indicators for a more balanced judgement.

front: What is GNI per capita?
p1: GNI per capita is the total value of goods and services produced by a country, plus net income from abroad, divided by the population.
p2: Nigeria is approximately $2,160 and the UK approximately $46,000+.
s: GNI per capita is the total value of goods and services produced by a country, plus net income from abroad, divided by the population.
Nigeria is approximately $2,160 and the UK approximately $46,000+.

front: What is the infant mortality rate?
p1: The infant mortality rate is the number of deaths of children under one year old per 1,000 live births.
p2: Nigeria is approximately 72 per 1,000 and the UK approximately 3.6 per 1,000.
s: The infant mortality rate is the number of deaths of children under one year old per 1,000 live births.
Nigeria is approximately 72 per 1,000 and the UK approximately 3.6 per 1,000.

front: What is the literacy rate?
p1: The literacy rate is the percentage of the population aged 15 and over who can read and write.
p2: Nigeria is approximately 62%, varying significantly between south and north, and the UK approximately 99%.
s: The literacy rate is the percentage of the population aged 15 and over who can read and write.
Nigeria is approximately 62%, varying significantly between south and north, and the UK approximately 99%.

front: What is life expectancy?
p1: Life expectancy is the average number of years a person is expected to live from birth.
p2: Nigeria is approximately 53 to 55 years and the UK approximately 81 years.
s: Life expectancy is the average number of years a person is expected to live from birth.
Nigeria is approximately 53 to 55 years and the UK approximately 81 years.

front: What is the Human Development Index?
p1: The Human Development Index is a composite statistic combining life expectancy, education and GNI per capita, scored 0 to 1.
p2: Nigeria scores approximately 0.54, medium human development, and the UK approximately 0.93, very high human development.
s: The Human Development Index is a composite statistic combining life expectancy, education and GNI per capita, scored 0 to 1.
Nigeria scores approximately 0.54, medium human development, and the UK approximately 0.93, very high human development.

front: What is access to safe water?
p1: Access to safe water is the percentage of the population with sustainable access to an improved water source.
p2: Around 64% of Nigerians have safely managed access, lower in rural regions such as the north, while in the UK virtually all households have treated tap water.
s: Access to safe water is the percentage of the population with sustainable access to an improved water source.
Around 64% of Nigerians have safely managed access, lower in rural regions such as the north, while in the UK virtually all households have treated tap water.

front: What are migration and push and pull factors?
p1: Migration is the movement of people from one place to another to live.
p2: A push factor makes people want to leave a place, such as low wages or conflict.
p3: A pull factor attracts people to a place, such as jobs or better services.
s: Migration is the movement of people from one place to another to live.
A push factor makes people want to leave a place, such as low wages or conflict.
A pull factor attracts people to a place, such as jobs or better services.

front: How do rural-urban and international migration differ?
p1: Rural-urban migration is the movement of people from the countryside to towns and cities, usually within one country.
p2: International migration is the movement of people from one country to another.
s: Rural-urban migration is the movement of people from the countryside to towns and cities, usually within one country.
International migration is the movement of people from one country to another.

front: What are economic migrants, remittances and brain drain?
p1: An economic migrant is someone who moves to find work or a higher income.
p2: Remittances are money that migrants send back to their families in their home country.
p3: Brain drain is the loss of skilled and educated workers, such as doctors, from a country.
s: An economic migrant is someone who moves to find work or a higher income.
Remittances are money that migrants send back to their families in their home country.
Brain drain is the loss of skilled and educated workers, such as doctors, from a country.

front: What are the multiplier effect and economic leakage?
p1: The positive multiplier effect is when spending creates jobs, which puts more money into the local economy.
p2: In tourism it can lead to better roads, airports and power.
p3: Economic leakage is when profits leak back to HICs such as the UK, where the TNC is based, rather than staying in Nigeria.
s: The positive multiplier effect is when spending creates jobs, which puts more money into the local economy.
In tourism it can lead to better roads, airports and power.
Economic leakage is when profits leak back to HICs such as the UK, where the TNC is based, rather than staying in Nigeria.

front: What is Fairtrade?
p1: Under Fairtrade, farmers get a fair, guaranteed price plus money for their community and better working conditions.
p2: Fairtrade products cost more.
s: Under Fairtrade, farmers get a fair, guaranteed price plus money for their community and better working conditions.
Fairtrade products cost more.

front: What is debt relief?
p1: Debt relief cancels or reduces money owed, freeing money for health and education.
p2: It often comes with conditions.
s: Debt relief cancels or reduces money owed, freeing money for health and education.
It often comes with conditions.

front: What is microfinance?
p1: Microfinance gives very small loans to people who are refused by banks.
p2: It empowers women, but interest can be high.
s: Microfinance gives very small loans to people who are refused by banks.
It empowers women, but interest can be high.

front: What is the Clark-Fisher model and what are the three job sectors?
p1: The Clark-Fisher model shows how, as a country develops, the way its people earn a living changes in a predictable order.
p2: Primary jobs are in agriculture, forestry and fishing; secondary jobs are in industry, such as manufacturing, mining, construction and utilities.
p3: Tertiary jobs are in services.
s: The Clark-Fisher model shows how, as a country develops, the way its people earn a living changes in a predictable order.
Primary jobs are in agriculture, forestry and fishing; secondary jobs are in industry, such as manufacturing, mining, construction and utilities.
Tertiary jobs are in services.

front: What is the demographic transition model?
p1: The demographic transition model shows how a population changes as a country develops; stage 1 has very high, fluctuating birth and death rates, so natural increase is very low.
p2: Stage 2 → death rate falls rapidly as healthcare, hygiene and living standards improve while birth rate stays high → population explosion; Nigeria's wide-based pyramid is a stage 2 shape.
p3: Stage 3 → birth rate falls rapidly as contraception becomes more available and more women work; stage 4 has low rates, with growth mainly from immigration; the UK is stage 4/5.

front: Where is Nigeria?
p1: Nigeria is in West Africa on the Gulf of Guinea, bordering Benin, Niger, Chad and Cameroon; it covers about 924,000 km², nearly four times the size of the UK.
p2: Abuja was purpose-built in the centre and became capital in 1991 → seen as neutral ground between the main ethnic groups; it replaced Lagos, still the biggest city.
p3: About 218 million people → the most populous country in Africa; more than 250 ethnic groups speak around 500 languages, with English official; Hausa, Yoruba and Igbo are the largest.

front: Why is Nigeria important?
p1: Culture: Nollywood is the second largest film industry in the world, Afrobeats has global audiences, and Wole Soyinka won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1986.
p2: Economy: once seen as Africa's largest, now third on the IMF's 2026 outlook; 70% work in agriculture; supplies 2.7% of the world's oil, the 12th largest producer.

front: How did history shape Nigeria's development?
p1: Britain ruled Nigeria from the mid-19th century until independence in 1960 → palm oil, peanuts and cocoa were extracted as raw materials, with no factories or education developed.
p2: It became a gate keeper state → wealth and power came only from controlling the 'gate', such as the port; European-drawn borders ignored ethnic, religious and cultural differences.
p3: Civil war lasted from 1967 to 1970, then dictatorships followed, with no stable democracy until 1999; the north suffers drought and desertification.

front: How does the development gap lead to migration?
p1: The gap in standard of living and wealth between richer and poorer countries drives migration; push factors include low wages or conflict, pull factors include jobs.
p2: In Kano and Sokoto over 70% live on under $1.90 a day; maternal mortality is about 917 per 100,000 against 512 nationally; the north has 0.24 doctors per 1,000, the south 1.3.

front: How can manufacturing and tourism help Nigeria?
p1: Nigeria's employment is about 34% primary, 18% secondary and 48% tertiary; the Clark-Fisher model shows how jobs change in a predictable order as a country develops.
p2: Tourism contributed about 4.5% of GDP in 2019 and employs 2.4 million; Lagos is the largest centre, with the Lekki beaches, and Badagry is linked to the Atlantic slave trade.

front: How else can aid and trade close the development gap?
p1: Official Development Assistance (ODA) passes from one government to another on a large scale; aid direct between governments is bilateral, aid through the World Bank is multilateral.
p2: Nigeria gets about 4% of Africa's aid; the World Bank gave $495 million for water management, including the Farin Ruwa dam; this aid is a loan, repaid with interest → debt.
p3: Problems → about $40 million is lost to corruption each year; up to 90% of ODA can be a loan; about $30 billion flows into Africa yearly but more flows out.

front: How do TNCs affect Nigeria?
p1: The Niger Delta is the centre of Nigeria's oil industry → about 50 oil fields, 5,000 km of pipelines and 90% of export income; Shell, Exxon, Chevron and Eni operate there.
p2: Positives → Shell employs over 4,500 directly and 20,000 indirectly, creating a multiplier effect; TNCs pay tax for schools and roads and bring new technology.
p3: Negatives → economic leakage as profits return to HICs; insecure jobs; about 240,000 barrels spilt a year, up to 25 years to clean.

front: What is a natural hazard?
p1: A natural hazard is a natural event that has the potential to threaten both life and property.
p2: Without people, natural events would be just that, events.
s: A natural hazard is a natural event that has the potential to threaten both life and property.
Without people, natural events would be just that, events.

front: What is a natural disaster?
p1: A hazard becomes a disaster when it affects people, causing injury, deaths and damage to goods, property and the environment.
p2: A disaster is a significant impact on a vulnerable population: 10 or more deaths, 100 or more people affected, or $1 million or more of economic loss.
s: A hazard becomes a disaster when it affects people, causing injury, deaths and damage to goods, property and the environment.
A disaster is a significant impact on a vulnerable population: 10 or more deaths, 100 or more people affected, or $1 million or more of economic loss.

front: What are geological and atmospheric hazards?
p1: Geological hazards are caused by land and tectonic processes.
p2: Atmospheric hazards are caused by weather and climate.
s: Geological hazards are caused by land and tectonic processes.
Atmospheric hazards are caused by weather and climate.

front: What affects hazard risk?
p1: The nature of the hazard matters: its type, its size (magnitude) and how often it occurs, which is its frequency.
p2: Vulnerability is higher when more people live in an area exposed to hazards, and poor populations often live in unsafe conditions.
p3: Capacity to cope is a country's ability to react, for example through evacuation and medical assistance.
s: The nature of the hazard matters: its type, its size (magnitude) and how often it occurs, which is its frequency.
Vulnerability is higher when more people live in an area exposed to hazards, and poor populations often live in unsafe conditions.
Capacity to cope is a country's ability to react, for example through evacuation and medical assistance.

front: What are tectonic plates and how do they move?
p1: A tectonic plate is part of the Earth's crust that floats on the mantle and can interact to cause earthquakes.
p2: Plates are thought to move because of convection currents in the mantle.
p3: These currents are created by heat from within the Earth.
s: A tectonic plate is part of the Earth's crust that floats on the mantle and can interact to cause earthquakes.
Plates are thought to move because of convection currents in the mantle.
These currents are created by heat from within the Earth.

front: What is a constructive plate margin?
p1: At a constructive margin convection currents drive plates apart, for example the Eurasian and North American plates at the Mid Atlantic Ridge.
p2: Magma rises through fissures to form submarine mountains and volcanoes; where the ridge rises above sea level, islands such as Iceland are created.
s: At a constructive margin convection currents drive plates apart, for example the Eurasian and North American plates at the Mid Atlantic Ridge.
Magma rises through fissures to form submarine mountains and volcanoes; where the ridge rises above sea level, islands such as Iceland are created.

front: What is a conservative plate margin?
p1: At a conservative margin the plates move past each other at different speeds or in different directions; they do not move apart.
p2: Friction makes the plates stick, pressure builds up, and when it is released it sends out huge amounts of energy as an earthquake.
p3: There are no volcanoes at a conservative margin; the San Andreas Fault is an example.
s: At a conservative margin the plates move past each other at different speeds or in different directions; they do not move apart.
Friction makes the plates stick, pressure builds up, and when it is released it sends out huge amounts of energy as an earthquake.
There are no volcanoes at a conservative margin; the San Andreas Fault is an example.

front: What is an earthquake?
p1: An earthquake is the sudden shaking of the Earth's crust due to the movement of the plates, and it usually lasts for a matter of seconds.
p2: Plates sometimes get stuck, so pressure builds up; when it is eventually released an earthquake tends to occur.
p3: Earthquakes happen along all plate boundaries.
s: An earthquake is the sudden shaking of the Earth's crust due to the movement of the plates, and it usually lasts for a matter of seconds.
Plates sometimes get stuck, so pressure builds up; when it is eventually released an earthquake tends to occur.
Earthquakes happen along all plate boundaries.

front: What are the focus and the epicentre?
p1: The point inside the crust where the pressure is released.
p2: The epicentre is the point on the Earth's surface directly above the focus.
p3: Earthquake waves are felt most strongly at the epicentre, becoming weaker as they travel further away.
s: The point inside the crust where the pressure is released.
The epicentre is the point on the Earth's surface directly above the focus.
Earthquake waves are felt most strongly at the epicentre, becoming weaker as they travel further away.

front: What is the Richter scale?
p1: The Richter scale measures the energy of an earthquake and is logarithmic, which means it measures shaking amplitude.
p2: The higher the magnitude, the less frequent the earthquake.
s: The Richter scale measures the energy of an earthquake and is logarithmic, which means it measures shaking amplitude.
The higher the magnitude, the less frequent the earthquake.

front: What is the Mercalli scale?

front: What are short and long term responses and what is an NGO?

front: What are the three Ps for reducing tectonic risk?

front: Can earthquakes be predicted?
p1: It is almost impossible to make accurate predictions about earthquakes because of a lack of warning signs.

front: What were the effects of the Kumamoto earthquakes?

front: What were the economic effects of the Kumamoto earthquakes?

front: What is global warming and how much has the Earth warmed?
p1: Global warming is the long-term change in the average weather patterns that have come to define Earth's local, regional and global climates.
p2: The planet's average surface temperature has risen about 1 degree Celsius since the late 19th century, a change driven largely by increased carbon dioxide emissions.

front: What is the short term evidence for climate change, and what are sediment cores?
p1: Temperature is measured directly using an instrument, and reliable thermometer records go back only about a hundred years in the UK.
p2: Ice sheets and Arctic sea ice have decreased in mass, glaciers are retreating almost everywhere, and sea levels have risen 20 cm in the last century.

front: What is an ice core and how far back do ice cores go?
p1: Ice cores are cylinders of ice drilled out of an ice sheet or glacier, mostly in Antarctica and Greenland.
p2: Small air bubbles trapped in the ice hold a sample of the past atmosphere, so we can measure past carbon dioxide, methane and nitrous oxide.
p3: The oldest continuous ice core records extend 123,000 years in Greenland and 800,000 years in Antarctica, and the longest cores reach 3 km in depth.

front: What are the natural causes of climate change?
p1: Earth's orbit around the Sun changes, which shifts the climate.
p2: Sun activity changes how much energy reaches the Earth.
p3: Volcanic eruptions release energy that can make the atmosphere temporarily hotter.

Volcanic eruptions release energy that can make the atmosphere temporarily hotter.

front: What are the greenhouse effects and carbon sinks?
p1: The natural greenhouse effect is when greenhouse gases at the edge of the atmosphere trap the Sun's heat, which helps sustain life on Earth.
p2: The enhanced greenhouse effect is when there are more greenhouse gases in the atmosphere, so more heat is trapped.
p3: A carbon sink is any natural environment, such as oceans and forests, that absorbs more carbon than it releases, and so lowers the concentration of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere.
s: The natural greenhouse effect is when greenhouse gases at the edge of the atmosphere trap the Sun's heat, which helps sustain life on Earth.

front: What are the human causes of climate change?
p1: Burning fossil fuels releases carbon dioxide, a greenhouse gas, which traps heat.
p2: Livestock farming produces methane, which traps heat more effectively than carbon dioxide.
p3: Deforestation removes carbon sinks, which are forests that absorb more carbon than they release.

front: Who is most responsible for climate change?
p1: Just 100 companies are the source of more than 70% of greenhouse gas emissions since 1988.
p2: More than half of global industrial emissions since 1988 trace back to just 25 companies, including ExxonMobil, Shell, BP and Chevron.

front: What is a feedback loop?
p1: Amazon wildfires release stored carbon back into the atmosphere, accelerating warming.
p2: The loss of forests reduces the Earth's ability to regulate climate, creating a feedback loop that worsens the situation.

front: What is the difference between mitigation and adaptation?
p1: Mitigation means stopping or reducing our greenhouse gas emissions to slow down the rate of climate change.
p2: Adaptation means changing the way we live to better suit our new environment.
s: Mitigation means stopping or reducing our greenhouse gas emissions to slow down the rate of climate change.
Adaptation means changing the way we live to better suit our new environment.

front: What is carbon capture and storage?
p1: Carbon capture and storage (CCS) captures carbon dioxide produced by industry and stores it underground so it cannot enter the atmosphere.
p2: It is still being developed and can be costly, but it could cut emissions from cement and steel manufacturing.

front: How can we adapt to climate change?
p1: Adaptation means changing how we live to suit the new environment; in farming this means changing to more resilient crop varieties and adjusting planting schedules.
p2: Managing water supply → rainwater harvesting, drip irrigation and sustainable groundwater management help communities use water efficiently in droughts.
p3: Reducing risk from rising sea levels → sea walls and flood barriers, plus restoring wetlands that absorb excess water.

p1: Rising seas threaten low-lying places such as the Maldives and parts of Bangladesh, where communities may be displaced.

front: What happens when precipitation falls?
p1: Precipitation is the process in which water, as rain, snow, sleet or hail, falls from clouds in the sky.
p2: Interception is when vegetation stops precipitation from reaching the ground.
p3: Accumulation is the process in which water gathers in large bodies such as oceans, seas and lakes.

front: How does water get into the atmosphere?
p1: Evaporation is the process in which liquid water becomes water vapour, from oceans, lakes, the land and melting snow fields.

front: What are infiltration, surface runoff and groundwater flow?
p1: Infiltration is the process whereby water enters the ground.
p2: Surface runoff is rain or snow melt that flows in surface streams, rivers or canals.
p3: Groundwater flow is rain or snow melt that flows in underground streams, drains or sewers.

front: What are discharge and velocity?
p1: Discharge is the amount of water in the river.
p2: Velocity is how fast the river flows.

front: What are erosion, transportation and deposition?
p1: Erosion is the breaking up and removal of rocks by the action of water.
p2: The broken rock is transported until, when the water loses energy, it is deposited.

front: What are hydraulic action, abrasion and attrition?
p1: Hydraulic action is when water is forced into cracks in the bank, weakening the rock until it breaks away.
p2: Abrasion is when rocks carried by the river rub against the bed and bank, wearing them away.
p3: Attrition is when rocks carried by the river smash together and break into smaller, smoother, rounder pebbles.

front: What are solution and suspension?

front: What are hydrological, atmospheric and tectonic hazards?
p1: Hydrological hazards are events related to water.
p2: Atmospheric hazards are caused by changes in the Earth's atmosphere and linked to weather and climate.
p3: Tectonic hazards are caused by the movement of tectonic plates beneath the Earth's crust.

Tectonic hazards are caused by the movement of tectonic plates beneath the Earth's crust.

front: What are the Coriolis effect and surface winds?
p1: The Coriolis effect results from the Earth's rotation, which distorts surface winds so they curve as they move from areas of high pressure to areas of low pressure.
p2: Surface winds transfer heat and moisture from one place to another, and they blow from high pressure zones to low pressure zones.

front: What is the Intertropical Convergence Zone?
p1: At the Equator the Sun's rays are very direct, so the warm air becomes less dense and rises.
p2: This creates an area of low pressure called the Intertropical Convergence Zone, where clouds form and heavy rainfall helps create the world's largest tropical rainforests.

front: What is the Hadley cell?
p1: In the Hadley cell, rising air travels at high altitude towards 30° north and south of the Equator, cools, becomes more dense and sinks.
p2: Where the air sinks high pressure creates clear skies and dry conditions, and at the surface air flows back towards the Equator as the trade winds.

front: What is a tropical storm?
p1: A tropical storm is a general term for rotating winds and clouds around a calm centre, forming over tropical or subtropical waters.
p2: Once its winds are stronger than 118 km/h it is called a hurricane, typhoon or cyclone, depending on where it originates.
s: A tropical storm is a general term for rotating winds and clouds around a calm centre, forming over tropical or subtropical waters.
Once its winds are stronger than 118 km/h it is called a hurricane, typhoon or cyclone, depending on where it originates.

front: Where and when do tropical storms form?
p1: Tropical storms form between about 5° and 30° latitude and do not occur directly on the Equator.
p2: They travel east to west, and their tracks bend away from the Equator, deflecting right in the northern hemisphere and left in the southern hemisphere.
p3: Hurricane season is July to October, cyclone season is January to April and typhoon season is July to October.
s: Tropical storms form between about 5° and 30° latitude and do not occur directly on the Equator.

Hurricane season is July to October, cyclone season is January to April and typhoon season is July to October.

front: How does a tropical storm form?
p1: Once the ocean water reaches at least 27°C, the air above is heated and rises quickly, causing an area of very low pressure.
p2: The rising air draws up more warm moist air, leading to strong winds, and it spirals upwards, cools and condenses into large cumulonimbus clouds.

front: What are the eye and the eye wall?
p1: In the centre of the storm, cold air sinks, forming the eye, where conditions are calm and dry.
p2: The large cumulonimbus clouds form the eye wall of the storm and produce heavy rainfall.
s: In the centre of the storm, cold air sinks, forming the eye, where conditions are calm and dry.

front: What is extreme weather, and why is the UK's weather so changeable?
p1: Extreme weather is when a weather event is significantly different from the average or usual weather patterns.
p2: The UK gets heatwaves, droughts, heavy rain, floods, strong winds, storms, snow and ice, and its weather is very changeable because different air masses affect it.
s: Extreme weather is when a weather event is significantly different from the average or usual weather patterns.
The UK gets heatwaves, droughts, heavy rain, floods, strong winds, storms, snow and ice, and its weather is very changeable because different air masses affect it.

front: What are immediate and long-term responses?
p1: Immediate responses are things urgently required in the hours or days after a disaster, often to reduce the negative effects.
p2: Long-term responses are to do with recovering and rebuilding after the disaster, which happens in the months and possibly years after.
s: Immediate responses are things urgently required in the hours or days after a disaster, often to reduce the negative effects.
Long-term responses are to do with recovering and rebuilding after the disaster, which happens in the months and possibly years after.

front: What are local, national and international responses?
p1: A local response is action taken by people or organisations in the affected area, such as residents, emergency services, hospitals and councils.
p2: A national response is organised by the country's government or national agencies, often involving large-scale funding, planning or deployment of resources.
p3: An international response is support from other countries or global organisations, such as aid agencies, charities, foreign governments or the United Nations.

front: How do tropical storms cause waterborne diseases?
p1: Waterborne diseases, such as cholera, are caused when water is contaminated with seawater, industrial waste or sewage.
p2: Storm surges cause flooding, which contaminates the water, and diseases such as cholera spread.

front: What conditions do tropical storms need?
p1: Sea surface temperature above 27°C to a depth of at least 60 m → intense evaporation saturates the air with water vapour.
p2: Trade winds converge near the Equator and force warm, moist air to rise → pressure falls; the rising air cools and condenses into cumulonimbus clouds.
p3: The Coriolis effect, caused by Earth's rotation, deflects incoming air and starts the spiral; storms do not form within about 5° of the Equator because the force is too weak.

front: How does a tropical storm develop and die?
p1: A tropical disturbance strengthens into a tropical depression, then a tropical storm, and eventually a tropical cyclone, hurricane or typhoon.
p2: At the centre is a calm eye of descending air; around it the eyewall has the strongest winds and heaviest rain; spiral rainbands draw in warm, moist air.
p3: Warm ocean water is the energy source; at landfall or over cooler water the energy supply is cut off → friction and loss of warm moisture weaken the storm.

front: What happened in Typhoon Haiyan?
p1: Haiyan struck the Philippines on 8 November 2013 (category 5); a storm surge and about 400 mm of rain flooded up to 1 km inland, destroying about 90% of Tacloban.
p2: Primary effects → power cut, airport damaged, roads blocked; three-quarters of farmers and fishers lost income; oil from a barge contaminated 10 hectares of mangrove.

front: How did people respond to Typhoon Haiyan?
p1: About 800,000 people were evacuated to stadiums in Tacloban, but some flooded; the Red Cross gave out rice and canned food; airport damage delayed aid by up to three days.

front: How can the effects of tropical storms be reduced?

front: How do UK heat and cold extremes compare?

front: What are primary, secondary and tertiary industry?
p1: Primary industry is acquiring raw materials from the earth, such as farming, cutting down trees, coal mining, oil drilling and fishing.
p2: Secondary industry is the manufacturing and assembly process, such as car factories, engineering and clothes factories.
p3: Tertiary industry is providing services, such as teachers, lawyers, doctors, politicians and waiters.

front: What is quaternary industry?
p1: Quaternary industry is providing information services, such as computing, ICT and research and development (R&D), especially in science.
p2: It is highly skilled service work requiring a high level of training and qualifications, and is sometimes included with the tertiary sector.
s: Quaternary industry is providing information services, such as computing, ICT and research and development (R&D), especially in science.

front: What are pre-industrial, industrial and post-industrial economies?
p1: A pre-industrial economy is a time before industrialisation, which in the UK means anytime before 1760.
p2: In an industrial economy the majority of jobs are connected to the processing of raw materials and the manufacture of goods in factories.
p3: A post-industrial economy is when a country no longer relies on heavy industry.

front: How did UK industry change?
p1: Industrialisation is the process by which an economy is transformed from primarily agricultural to one based on the manufacturing of goods.
p2: Mechanisation means employment in the primary sector decreases as machines replace manual labour, so manual labour in the collieries became unnecessary.

front: What is nationalisation?
p1: Nationalised industries, such as collieries, are publicly owned.
p2: Over-employment in publicly owned companies such as collieries led to mass unemployment from the 1960s onwards.

front: What are financial services?
p1: Financial services are any businesses that manage money, including banks, credit-card companies, insurance companies, accountancy companies and hedge funds.
p2: Many of these jobs are based in the City of London, a small area of central London, also known as the Square Mile.

front: What are footloose industries and circular economies?
p1: A footloose industry can be placed at any location without effect from factors such as resources.

front: What are science parks and business parks?
p1: Science parks are located near university sites, where high-tech industries are established.
p2: Scientific research and commercial development may be carried out in co-operation with the university.
p3: Business parks are purpose built areas of offices, often at the edge of a city on a main road.

front: What is the north-south divide and how do government policies reduce it?
p1: The north-south divide is the economic, cultural and political differences between the north and south of England, with the south perceived as more affluent.
p2: Regional aid, freeports, devolved parliaments and directly elected mayors transfer political and economic power away from the UK's south.

front: How do two rural areas in the UK contrast, and who commutes?
p1: A commuter is somebody who travels in to and out of a city each day for work.
p2: Hurstpierpoint in West Sussex is a rural commuter town in south east England with a rapidly growing population.
p3: Capel Dewi in south Wales is an ex-mining village with a rapidly declining population.

front: What is infrastructure?
p1: Infrastructure is the basic structures and connections, such as roads, utilities, transport, water supply and sewage, that a country needs to function properly.
p2: It is widely accepted that there is a pro-London bias when it comes to transport in the UK.

front: How is the UK linked to the world politically, and how has globalisation affected manufacturing?
p1: The UK is linked to the world politically through the Commonwealth, the G7 and the UN Security Council.
p2: Improvements in transport and new trade policies with industrial economies abroad make British manufacturing uncompetitive.
p3: With higher wages and unit costs of production, coal is cheaper to import from abroad.

front: Why did the coal industry in South Wales decline?
p1: Mechanisation made manual labour in the collieries unnecessary, and nationalisation propped up the industry for longer than it should have without giving miners alternative careers.
p2: Globalisation made UK coal uncompetitive, because with higher wages and unit costs of production it was cheaper to import coal from abroad.

front: What are the social impacts of deindustrialisation?
p1: Skilled workers leave, which causes migration and a brain drain.
p2: Levels of crime increase, and family tensions and breakdown rise.
p3: Drug use and alcoholism increase.

front: What are the economic impacts of deindustrialisation?
p1: Workers lose income, and local shops and services lose income too.
p2: High unemployment means rising demand for income-support benefits, and the government loses income tax.
p3: A poor image puts off new investors, so there is no new investment and the local economy declines.

front: What are the environmental impacts of deindustrialisation?
p1: Derelict land is very unattractive, and empty factory buildings attract litter.

front: How has the UK moved from manufacturing to financial services?

front: Why is the M4 corridor a good location for science and research parks?

front: How do the north and south of the UK differ?
p1: The north is more deprived, has higher unemployment and had most manufacturing industry before deindustrialisation.
p2: The south is less deprived, and includes London as a global business hub and almost all of the UK's most economically successful towns, such as Oxford and Cambridge.
p3: Out-migration of young, educated and skilled workers from the north causes a brain drain.
